title: Designing a Content Moderation Pipeline: Automated Filters, Human Review, and Appeals
lesson:
A content moderation system decides whether user-generated content (posts, images, videos, comments) is allowed, and acts on that decision. The scale problem is that millions of items arrive per hour while human reviewers can only handle a tiny fraction, so the design is layered: cheap, fast checks run first and expensive or human checks run only on what remains uncertain.

The typical pipeline has a synchronous pre-publish stage and an asynchronous post-publish stage. Pre-publish checks must be fast and cheap: hash matching against known-bad content (exact hashes and perceptual hashes that survive resizing or re-encoding), blocklists, and rule-based filters. Heavier ML classifiers for nudity, violence, hate speech, or spam usually run asynchronously off a queue, because model inference on video is slow. Each classifier emits a score, and thresholds route the item: high-confidence violations are removed automatically, low scores are published, and the uncertain middle band goes to a human review queue.

Human review queues need real engineering. Items are prioritised by severity and by expected reach (a post going viral matters more than one with no views), assigned to reviewers by language and skill, and given a lease so two reviewers do not work on the same item while a stuck item is returned to the queue. Reviewer decisions are also labelled training data, which feeds back into the classifiers. Reviewer wellbeing matters too, for example blurring graphic media by default and limiting exposure.

Every decision should be recorded as an immutable audit trail with the policy version, the signals involved, and who or what made the call. This supports appeals, where a user contests a removal and a different reviewer re-evaluates it, and it allows enforcement to be reversed cleanly. Policies change over time, so decisions are tied to a policy version, and the system can re-scan existing content when a new rule or a better model ships. Thresholds trade precision against recall: a lower removal threshold catches more abuse but wrongly removes more legitimate content, so the uncertain band is the main lever for balancing them against reviewer capacity.

questions.prompt: Why are heavy ML video classifiers usually run asynchronously rather than before publishing?
options: Inference on video is slow and would add unacceptable publish latency
Asynchronous models are always more accurate
Synchronous checks are forbidden by regulation
Classifiers cannot read video files synchronously
questions.explanation: Slow, expensive inference is moved off the request path onto a queue so publishing stays fast, while cheap checks still run inline.

questions.prompt: Perceptual hashing can match a re-encoded or resized copy of known-bad media, which an exact cryptographic hash would miss.
questions.explanation: Cryptographic hashes change completely on any byte difference, whereas perceptual hashes map visually similar content to similar values.

questions.prompt: Items whose classifier score falls between the auto-allow and auto-remove thresholds are routed to a ____ queue.
questions.explanation: The uncertain middle band is where automation is least reliable, so people make the final call.

questions.prompt: Order the stages of handling a newly uploaded post, earliest first.
items: Uncertain items are placed in a prioritised human review queue
Cheap inline checks run (hash match, blocklist)
Async ML classifiers score the content
questions.explanation: Fast inline checks come first, then slower async scoring, and only the uncertain remainder reaches humans.

questions.prompt: Why should each moderation decision record the policy version and signals used?
options: To support appeals, audits, and reversing or re-evaluating decisions when policy changes
questions.explanation: An audit trail tied to a policy version lets reviewers explain, contest, and correct decisions later.
